one_liner: Learned eviction (XGBoost over write-time object groups): higher hit ratio than LRU, slower than LRU, 228x faster than LRB.
what_it_does: GL-Cache is a learned cache-eviction policy from a FAST'23 paper (CMU, Yale, Pelikan Foundation). It aims to beat LRU and hand-tuned heuristics on hit ratio while costing much less CPU and memory than object-level learned caches such as LRB. The maintained code is the `glcache` eviction module in libCacheSim, a C cache-simulation library. You create it through libCacheSim's cache_t get/find/insert/evict interface or run `cachesim <trace> <type> glcache <size>`, replay a trace and get hit/miss counts; it keeps metadata only and stores no values. The paper's artifact repo also has a single-binary Rust prototype built on a 2022 snapshot of Pelikan Segcache.
how_it_is_fast: It uses group-level learning. Objects are grouped by write time into fixed-size segments, laid out like a log as in Segcache. A gradient-boosted tree model (XGBoost, regression with squared-error loss, retrained from scratch once a day) predicts each group's utility, defined as the sum over its objects of 1/(time to next access x size), from 6-7 cheap group features: age, mean object size, hits, active objects, and the request rate, miss ratio and write rate when the group was created. One inference ranks all groups and is reused until a fraction F_eviction (2-10%) of them has been evicted. Each eviction merges the lowest-utility group with its N_merge-1 neighbours in write time and keeps only the best objects, scored by 1/(size x age). Per-object metadata is about 5 bytes (a 4-byte last-access time plus under 1 byte of amortized group features), against 16 for LRU's list pointers and 189-192 for LRB. A hit only updates the access time, plus the utility for groups sampled for training.
when_to_use: Simulating or evaluating eviction policies on block-I/O or CDN traces in libCacheSim, where hit ratio matters more than CPU per request (in the paper, LRU and Cacheus gained only single-digit % over FIFO on the median trace; GL-Cache gained much more)
You want a learned eviction policy but cannot afford LRB: GL-Cache-E is 228x faster than LRB on average at the small cache size, GL-Cache-T 586x, with a 7% higher mean hit ratio
Segment or log-structured caches (Segcache-style) where evicting whole segments is natural: on one CloudPhysics trace the prototype raised hit ratio by 60% over plain Segcache at 8 GB
Variable-size objects and workloads whose mix of recency, frequency and size changes with cache size (the model re-weights features per trace and per cache size)
Traces with real timestamps covering several days, since training uses wall-clock intervals (first model after one day of trace time, then daily retraining)
when_not_to_use: If you need more requests per second than LRU gives: in the micro-implementation LRU runs close to FIFO, while GL-Cache runs at 0.3-0.8x FIFO (paper Table 1), and GL-Cache-E reaches only 2.55-4.20 MQPS against FIFO's 7.62-9.68 on the Wikimedia trace
Short traces or ones without meaningful timestamps: until the first model is trained (one day of trace time) it evicts segments in plain FIFO order
As a production in-process cache: the libCacheSim module is a metadata-only simulator policy with no locking and no value storage, and the Rust prototype is a research benchmark frozen since May 2023

Builds that cannot take on an XGBoost dependency or an opt-in build flag: GLCache compiles only with -DENABLE_GLCACHE=ON, CI never builds or tests it, and XGBoost installs have broken on macOS (issue #180)

Latency-sensitive paths: libCacheSim calls train() synchronously inside get() (10-50 ms per training in the paper) and runs inference inside eviction (0.4-3 ms), and each group eviction removes hundreds to thousands of objects at once

integration.form: shared lib (the glcache C module inside libCacheSim, built only with -DENABLE_GLCACHE=ON; BUILD_SHARED_LIBS defaults to ON)
integration.dependencies: XGBoost C API (find_package(xgboost) REQUIRED when enabled), glib, zstd, tcmalloc (per README), CMake; the Rust prototype uses a fork of rust-xgboost (1a1a11a/rust-xgboost) and forks of Twitter's rustcommon
integration.min_toolchain: CMake 3.12+ with a C compiler (C standard not stated; C++17 set for libCacheSim's C++ parts); prototype: Rust 2021 edition
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS (libCacheSim CI builds both, but without GLCache; PR #280 in July 2025 fixed compiling GL-Cache on macOS)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The GLCache sources have no locks, keep some static state, and train XGBoost with nthread=1 inside the request path, so use one cache instance per thread.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — inside libCacheSim it swaps for the `lru` policy by name through the same cache_t interface, but it is a simulator policy with no value storage, so no library can replace an application's LRU cache with it

gotchas: libCacheSim's defaults (segment-size=100, n-merge=2, rank-intvl=0.02, retrain-intvl=86400) match neither paper configuration (GL-Cache-E: 60 objects/2/0.02; GL-Cache-T: 200/5/0.1). Set parameters explicitly to reproduce the paper.

The code has drifted from the paper: the GLCache README says it retrains every two days but the code default is one day, and libCacheSim uses 6 features, dropping write rate as redundant, where the paper lists 7. It runs 20 boosting rounds; the Rust prototype runs 8.
Bad parameters: an unknown key makes the parser call exit(1), and the range checks are assert() calls, which disappear in NDEBUG builds.

The artifact's license is unclear: GitHub detects no license for Thesys-lab/fast23-GLCache, its README says Apache-2.0, and micro-implementation/LICENSE is GPL-3.0. Use the libCacheSim copy, which is Apache-2.0 (relicensed in PR #324 on 2026-09-13).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick GL-Cache over LRB when you want learned eviction without LRB's per-object cost: it is 228-586x faster with a similar or higher hit ratio. Pick it over LHD or Cacheus when hit ratio on diverse block traces matters: up to 37.8% above LHD, and 60% higher on the median MSR trace at the small cache size. Pick S3-FIFO or SIEVE (same repo) instead when you need throughput and multi-threaded scaling beyond LRU and no ML dependency.
verified_claims_summary: The FAST'23 paper replays 118 production traces (103 CloudPhysics and 14 MSR block-I/O traces, plus 1 Wikimedia CDN trace) in a closed loop. In the libCacheSim micro-implementation (CloudLab m510, Xeon D-1548; compiler and flags not stated), GL-Cache raises hit ratio well above LRU's single-digit gain over FIFO but runs slower than LRU, and its throughput wins (228x/586x over LRB, 64% over the fastest other learned cache) are against learned caches, not LRU. In the Segcache-based Rust prototype (CloudLab c6420, Xeon Gold 6142, one CloudPhysics trace, release profile opt-level 3 with LTO), it gets up to 40% higher hit ratio than the best baseline, at throughput similar to Cachelib's throughput-optimized LRU and to Segcache.
status_note: libCacheSim is actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-26, Apache-2.0, 347 stars), and the GLCache sources were last touched 2026-09-13. The module is still opt-in, untested in CI and simulator-only, and the paper's Thesys-lab artifact has been frozen since 2023-05-12.
